The Third Conditional - Talking Hypothetically About the Past

You use the third conditional to talk about unreal situations in the past.
These are things that did not happen in the past. You often use the third conditional to talk about regrets.
When you want to talk about situations in the past in a hypothetical context (not real or necessarily true), you can use the structures would have, should have and could have.
Could have (+ past participle) means that it was possible to do something at a time in the past, or you had the ability to do something, however, you did not do it.
If I had explained why I deserved a lead, he could have considered it.

Should have (+ past participle) means that you had some obligation to do something in the past, or that it may have been a good idea to do something, however, you did not do it. Should have can also express regret about something you did or did not do.
If I had known how ungrateful he was going to be, I should have just said I'd leave the company.
Use would have (+ past participle) to speculate about the past.
If I had prepared more, he would have said yes immediately.

Talking About the Past: The Simple Past, The Present Perfect and the Past Continuous Tenses
When you tell stories and anecdotes, it is common to use a mixture of tenses. The allows you to convey a variety of timelines and action sequences.
You use the Simple Past tense to talk about many different types of events in the past: short, quickly finished actions, longer situations and repeated events.

Finally, Tom went into the production office.
Last month, he decided that the time had come to ask for a leading role.

You use the Present Perfect tense to talk about a past action or an action that began in the past that is connected to the present in some way. It is common to use for and since when referring to time periods in the Present Perfect.

He has been a hard worker.
Tom's been an actor with the theater company for two years.
You use the Past Continuous tense to talk about an action that was happening at a time before now and to describe the background in a story written in the past tense.

While he was standing there, frustrated, he blurted out, "I think I deserve a leading role!."
Tom was feeling so distressed that he dashed out of the office.

images.text:
Tom's been an actor with the theater company for two years. He has been a hard worker. He's earned a lot of recognition for his supporting roles. Last month, he decided that the time had come to ask for a leading role. Every morning he decided that he was asking today. Every afternoon he put it off. Finally, Tom went into the production office. He completely forgot what he was planning to say. While he was standing there, frustrated, he blurted out, "I think I deserve a leading role!"
The producer seemed surprised by this unexpected outburst. "Sorry, Tom," he said. "This isn't the right time."

Tom was feeling so distressed that he dashed out of the office. As soon as he stepped out, he regretted saying anything. "If I had prepared more, he would have said yes immediately, "Tom thought to himself. "If I had explained why I deserved a lead, he could have considered it. If I hadn't said I deserved it, he may have been more open to the idea".

As the day wore on, Tom got angry. "If I had threatened to quit, he would have changed his tune," Tom muttered to himself. "If I had known how ungrateful he was going to be, I should have just said I'd leave the company." Tom got up with determination and went into the production office again. The producer looked up. He was smiling. "Tom," he said. "I've got time now. You're right, I've been meaning to feature you this season!”
